questions.stem: Which level of organisation sits directly above cells in the hierarchy?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Organelles sit below cells — they are the parts inside one.
An organ is two rungs up, built from several tissues.
A system is the top rung, a team of organs.
Organelles are discrete structures, not the fluid around them.

options.text: A specialised structure inside a cell that carries out one particular job
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A group of similar cells doing one job
options.explanation: That defines a tissue, not a cell part.

options.text: A structure built from several tissues
options.explanation: That is the definition of an organ.

questions.stem: At which single level of organisation would the heart alone be placed?

options.explanation: The heart alone is not a system — it is one member of the circulatory system.
The heart is far too large and complex to be a single cell.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The heart is not one repeated cell type; it contains muscle, nerve and connective tissues.

questions.stem: Which statement about unicellular organisms is correct?

options.explanation: That describes multicellular organisms.

options.text: They are built from tissues working together
options.explanation: Tissues require many cells; unicellular organisms have just one.
Even single cells house organelles such as the nucleus.

options.text: Their single cell must carry out every life process the organism needs
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which sequence orders cell, tissue, organ and system by increasing complexity?

options.text: Cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Tissue, then cell, then organ, then organ system
options.explanation: A tissue cannot come before the cells that form it.

options.text: Cell, then organ, then tissue, then organ system
options.explanation: Organs are assembled from tissues, so tissue must come first.

options.text: Organ system, then organ, then tissue, then cell
options.explanation: That is the decreasing order, not increasing.

questions.stem: Define a tissue in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to carry out one particular function.

questions.stem: Name the five levels of organisation in order, starting with the smallest.
questions.modelAnswer: Organelles, then cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems.

questions.stem: Explain why multicellular organisms need specialised cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a single unspecialised cell could not perform every job a whole body demands; specialisation lets each cell type become efficient at one task, and the different specialists then combine into tissues, organs and systems that divide the workload between them.

questions.stem: A leaf is called an organ. Justify this by naming the level found directly below it.
questions.modelAnswer: An organ is a structure assembled from several different tissues, and a leaf contains tissues such as mesophyll and epidermis working on one job; those tissues in turn consist of specialised leaf cells, so the level directly below the leaf organ is tissue.

questions.stem: Which organelle is named as the site of aerobic respiration?

options.explanation: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The nucleus stores genetic material; respiration happens elsewhere.
Ribosomes build proteins, not respiration.

questions.stem: Which organ system contains the leaf, stem and flower as its organs?

options.explanation: That system handles trachea and lungs.
Lungs, kidneys and skin serve excretion.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Roots and tubers belong to the root system.

questions.stem: Xylem and phloem appear in the tissue column of both plant systems. What are they?

options.explanation: They are listed in the tissue column, below the organ level.
They are macroscopic structures, not cell parts.
A single transport tissue is not a whole system.

options.text: Tissues that transport substances around the plant
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: The digestive, circulatory and respiratory systems share which tissue examples?

options.text: Muscle, connective, nerve and epithelial tissues
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those are plant transport tissues.
Those belong to leaves.
Those are leaf structures, not the listed tissue set.

questions.stem: Which pairing of system to organs is correct according to the table?

options.explanation: Ovary, uterus and testes belong to reproduction.

options.text: Excretory system — lungs, kidneys and skin
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The nervous system lists brain and spinal cord.
The circulatory system lists the heart.

questions.stem: State the definition of an organ system given in the table.
questions.modelAnswer: A set of organs cooperating on one overall function — that is the table's definition.

questions.stem: Name two organs of the root system and one tissue found in it.
questions.modelAnswer: The root and the tuber are its organs, and xylem or phloem are tissues found there.

questions.stem: Explain why the heart is listed as an organ rather than a tissue.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the heart is built from several different tissues — muscle, connective, nerve and epithelial — cooperating on one job, and an organ is exactly that combination, whereas a tissue would be many similar cells of one type.

questions.stem: A surgeon biopsies a small patch of stomach muscle. Place the sample, the stomach and digestion in order of organisational level.
questions.modelAnswer: The sample of muscle is a tissue, the stomach is an organ built from tissues, and digestion is carried out by the digestive system, a group of cooperating organs.
